items.text: AMEND AND RECOMMIT TO ENERGY AND TELECOMMUNICATIONS

items.actClause:
AN ACT to amend the public service law, in relation to the transfer of bill
credits associated with the electricity produced by community distributed
generation facilities
items.memo:
BILL NUMBER: S3521

SPONSOR: PARKER
 
TITLE OF BILL:

An act to amend the public service law, in relation to the transfer of
bill credits associated with the electricity produced by community
distributed generation facilities

 
PURPOSE OR GENERAL IDEA OF BILL:

This bill would define "community distributed generation facility" in
public service law, and direct the Public Service Commission to create a
system of tariffs and accounting practices to provide for the transfer
of bill credits from community distributed generation projects in one
utility territory to the accounts of subscribers in another.

 
SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS:

Section 1: Amends the public service law by adding a new section 66-q
that defines the term "community distributed generation facility" and
establishes a system of credits that participating electric customers
shall receive. Additionally, this section specifies the process the
Public Service Commission shall follow to direct electric corporations
to file a model tariff to provide for the transfer of bill credits from
community distributed generation facilities in one electric corporation
territory to the accounts of subscribers in other electric corporation
territories, as well as the approval of such tariffs to enable such
transfer.

Section 2: The effective date.

 
JUSTIFICATION:

Despite the best intentions of the State's efforts to achieve a goal of
3 GWs of solar-generated electricity, as well as current efforts to at
least double that total, there are pockets of the state that have not
been able to participate in these environmentally and economically bene-
ficial initiatives. Because of a lack of rooftop access and/or suffi-
ciently sized parcels, the benefits of participating in local solar
generation have not been available to those in more densely-populated
areas, including many lower-income communities.

Community distributed generation, the most common form of which is
community solar, is a form of renewable energy development designed to
expand the benefits to all.

Community solar refers to local solar facilities shared by multiple
community subscribers who receive credit on their electricity bills for
their share of the power produced. This model for solar is rapidly being
adopted nationwide.

According to the Coalition for Community Solar Access, "today, only a
small minority of American households and businesses have access to
solar because they rent, live in multi tenant buildings, have roofs that
are unable to host a solar system, are shaded by trees or experience
some other mitigating factor."


By enabling customers in one utility territory to participate in commu-
nity distributed generation projects located in another utility territo-
ry, the state can maximize efficient deployment of solar generation
resources while ensuring that all New Yorkers have an equitable opportu-
nity to participate in these projects.  In particular, customers living
in areas with high population and building density would be better able
to participate in solar energy projects, while ensuring project siting
is cost-effective and can contribute to much-needed economic development
initiatives in local communities.

 
PRIOR LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:

2019/20 S5627 -     ORDERED TO THIRD READING CAL.996
                    PASSED SENATE
                    DELIVERED TO ASSEMBLY
                    Referred to ways and means

 
FISCAL IMPLICATIONS FOR STATE AND LOCAL GOVERNMENTS:

None. The Public Service Commission would need to authorize an account-
ing system to accommodate the transfer of bill credits between utili-
ties.

 
EFFECTIVE DATE:
This act shall take effect immediately.

A.memo:
BILL NUMBER: S3521A

SPONSOR: PARKER
 
TITLE OF BILL:

An act to amend the public service law, in relation to the transfer of
bill credits associated with the electricity produced by community
distributed generation facilities

 
PURPOSE OR GENERAL IDEA OF BILL:

This bill would define "community distributed generation facility" in
public service law, and direct the Public Service Commission to create a
system of tariffs and accounting practices to provide for the transfer
of bill credits from community distributed generation projects in one
utility territory to the accounts of subscribers in another, providing
35 percent of the benefits of those facilities to disadvantaged communi-
ties.

 
SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS:

Section 1: Names the bill the "Community Solar for Disadvantaged Commu-
nities Act"

Section 2: Legislative Intent. Leading-edge goal to build 6 gigawatts
(GW) of distributed solar generation by 2025, and to provide benefits to
disadvantaged communities through the provision of low-cost renewable
power.

Section 3: Amends the public service law by adding a new section 66-q
that defines the term "community distributed generation facility" and
establishes a system of credits that participating electric customers
shall receive. Additionally, this section specifies the process the
Public Service Commission shall follow to direct electric corporations
to file a model tariff to provide for the transfer of bill credits from
community distributed generation facilities in one electric corporation
territory to the accounts of subscribers in other electric corporation
territories, as well as the approval of such tariffs to enable such
transfer.

Section 4: Amends the public service law by adding a new Section 66-r to
extend the CDGFBC to disadvantaged communities. At least 35% of the
customer credits shall be provided to disadvantaged communities.  Commu-
nity Solar Project developers must designate to the PSC which of their
facilities are participating in this program, then providing 35% of the
benefits from all their participating facilities to disadvantaged commu-
nities.

 
JUSTIFICATION:

In the Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act (CLCPA), the
State doubled to 6 GW - the State's goal for solar-generated electric-
ity, and in the same law, encouraged the extension of the benefits of
such projects to disadvantaged communities.

However, there are pockets of the state that have not been able to
participate in these environmentally and economically beneficial initi-
atives due to a lack of rooftop access and/or sufficiently sized
parcels. This has meant the benefits of participating in solar gener-
ation have not been available to those in more densely-populated areas,
especially many lower-income communities.

Community distributed generation, the most common form of which is
community solar, is a form of renewable energy development designed to
expand the benefits to all.

Community solar refers to local solar facilities shared by multiple
community subscribers who receive credit on their electricity bills for
their share of the power produced. This model for solar is rapidly being
adopted nationwide.

According to the Coalition for Community Solar Access, "today, only a
small minority of American households and businesses have access to
solar because they rent, live in multi-tenant buildings, have roofs that
are unable to host a solar system, are shaded by trees or experience
some other mitigating factor."

By enabling customers in one utility territory to participate in commu-
nity distributed generation projects located in another utility territo-
ry, the state can maximize efficient deployment of solar generation
resources while ensuring that all New Yorkers have an equitable opportu-
nity to participate in these projects. In particular, customers living
in areas with high population and building density would be better able
to participate in solar energy projects, while ensuring project siting
is cost-effective and can contribute to much-needed economic development
initiatives in local communities.

 
PRIOR LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:

2021-22: S3521 - REFERRED TO ENERGY AND TELECOMMUNICATIONS
2019-20: S5627 - ORDERED TO THIRD READING CAL.996
                 PASSED SENATE
                 DELIVERED TO ASSEMBLY
                 referred to ways and means

 
FISCAL IMPLICATIONS:

None. The Public Service Commission would need to authorize an account-
ing system to accommodate the transfer of bill credits between utili-
ties.

 
EFFECTIVE DATE:
This act shall take effect immediately.

summary: Expands customer access to community distributed generation by creating a model tariff to provide for the transfer of bill credits associated with electricity produced by community distributed generation facilities in one electric corporation territory to other territories.
title: Relates to expanding customer access to community distributed generation

items.memoText:
VETO MESSAGE - No. 75
 
TO THE SENATE:
 
I am returning herewith, without my approval, the following bill:
 
Senate Bill Number 3521-A, entitled:
 
    "AN ACT to amend the public service law, in relation to the transfer
      of bill credits associated with the electricity produced by commu-
      nity distributed generation facilities"
 
    NOT APPROVED
 
  This  bill  would  amend  the  Public  Service  Law (PSL) to add a new
section 66-q to require  the  Public  Service  Commission  (Commission),
within  90  days of the bill's immediate effective date, to direct elec-
tric corporations to file a model tariff providing for the  transfer  of
bill  credits associated with electricity produced by community distrib-
uted generation photovoltaic (community solar) facilities in  one  elec-
tric corporation territory to the accounts of subscribers in other util-
ity  service territories, and any other settlement systems and processes
necessary to effectuate such transfers. The bill  further  directs  that
the  Commission,  within  270 days of the bill's effective date, approve
tariffs to enable such transfers. The bill also states that  participat-
ing  electric  customers  "receive"  a  bill  credit for the electricity
generated in proportion to the size of their interest in  the  facility,
with  at least 60% of the facility's production allocated to participat-
ing customers in increments of 25 kilowatts or less.
 
  In addition, this bill would add a new PSL  Section  66-r  to  require
that community solar facilities that are designated for participation in
the  cross-utility  crediting  (CUC)  system  established under proposed
section 66-q provide at least 35% of  the  credits  from  the  aggregate
generation  resulting from the designated projects under their ownership
to disadvantaged communities.
 
  The bill would also, among other things, authorize the  Commission  to
review  the compensation mechanisms for community solar facilities sited
within the City of New York to ensure that the market is  achieving  its
potential.
 
  I  agree  with the underlying intent of this bill, which is to provide
additional opportunities for New Yorkers in urban  areas  to  enjoy  the
benefits of community solar. However, I am concerned that this bill will
have  the  unintended  consequences of impeding development of community
solar facilities throughout the state, including our  urban  areas,  and
increasing  costs to ratepayers who would receive no corresponding bene-
fits, and would result in other inequities.
 
  Preliminarily, the CUC system this bill would  create  conflicts  with
the  concept  of  "community" solar because it would allow ratepayers in
one utility area to participate as customers of community solar  facili-
ties  built  in  other utility areas, including facilities that could be
sited hundreds of  miles  away.  As  the  bill's  supporting  memorandum
acknowledges:   "Community solar refers to local solar facilities shared
by multiple community subscribers who receive credit on their  electric-
ity bills for their share of the power produced." Similarly, the bill is
 
inconsistent  with  the policy underlying the state's existing programs,
including NY Sun, which is to align the  program's  costs  and  benefits
with the specific communities where the solar facilities are located.
 
  While  the bill declares that its provisions "shall not impede" commu-
nity solar development within  New  York  City,  I  share  the  concerns
expressed  by  some  stakeholders,  including the City of New York, that
this bill stands to diminish incentives for development in  urban  areas
like  New  York  City  by  encouraging development in areas of the state
where project economics are more favorable. This result would be contra-
ry to the state's policy to support community solar development through-
out the state. Moreover, it would deny residents in urban areas like New
York City other benefits associated with community solar projects,  such
as  local  job  creation,  economic  development opportunities for local
businesses, and development of "home grown" clean  energy  solutions  to
enable neighborhoods to help chart their own course for a cleaner, heal-
thier and more resilient community.
 
  In  addition,  I  am  concerned  that  this legislation will result in
upstate ratepayers subsidizing the energy  costs  of  downstate  partic-
ipants,  while  also  bearing  the  costs  associated  with  things like
distribution system upgrades necessary to accommodate  solar  facilities
built  in  their  communities,  as well as the brunt of construction and
other impacts  associated  with  development  of  facilities  and  other
infrastructure.  This  could, in turn, discourage upstate municipalities
from approving community solar facilities over concerns that the facili-
ties would not benefit their communities.
 
  I share the sponsors' concerns that the State can do more  to  support
the development of community solar in the state's urban areas, especial-
ly  in  disadvantaged  communities.  Indeed,  on  September  20, 2021, I
announced a vast expansion of  the  NY  Sun  program,  with  a  specific
mandate  that at least 35 percent of the benefits of the expansion go to
disadvantaged  communities  and  low-to  moderate-income  New   Yorkers.
Consistent  with  my  announcement, the Department of Public Service and
the New York  State  Energy  Research  and  Development  Authority  have
prepared  a  proposal that was issued for public comment on December 17,
2021, to achieve at least 10 gigawatts of distributed solar by 2023, and
require at least 450 megawatts of residential, commercial and  community
solar to be sited in urban areas like New York City_ Further, on October
20,  2021,  I  announced  signed agreements for the development of solar
arrays and energy storage at 47 public schools and several water  treat-
ment  facilities  in  New York City that will reduce citywide emissions.
These initiatives confirm my  administration's  commitment  to  ensuring
that  all  areas  of  the State experience the benefits of solar energy,
including community solar, as well as the  State's  other  clean  energy
programs. However, I will ask the Department of Public Service to evalu-
ate  options to further the goals of the sponsors in this legislation in
a way that will equitably expand availability of community solar facili-
ties.
 
  The bill is disapproved.                       (signed) KATHY HOCHUL
 
                               __________
